claims.text: Targeted elemental substitution that increases atomic size mismatch increases local lattice distortion in single-phase multi-component concentrated alloys.
Greater local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion through increased dislocation pinning.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice distortion raises yield strength.
Increasing atomic size mismatch alters work-hardening behavior.
Increasing lattice distortion raises the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation.
Lattice strain affects dislocation-core energetics and stacking-fault behavior in concentrated alloys.
Enhanced lattice distortion promotes dislocation pinning.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than baseline alloys with minimal mismatch.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will have lower dislocation mobility than baseline alloys.
Alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will show more pronounced work hardening than baseline alloys.
Work hardening occurs in related single-phase refractory concentrated alloys at elevated temperatures.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism should operate from ambient to elevated temperatures and over varying strain rates.
Related single-phase BCC refractory concentrated alloys retain phase stability and substantial strength at elevated temperatures.
Lattice-distortion strengthening dominates when grain-boundary and second-phase contributions are minimal.
Short-range ordering may independently affect deformation behavior.
A lack of statistically significant differences in strength, work hardening, and dislocation pinning between high- and low-mismatch series would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
